newsitem.title: USA: Cold storage report supportive to pork futures.
newsitem.headline: Cold storage report supportive to pork futures.

text.p: USDA's monthly Cold Storage report should be supportive to pork futures, especially pork bellies, because of a much lower than expected amount of product in storage, analysts said.

CME pork belly futures are seen opening 0.500 to 2.000 cents per lb or more higher on Monday following the report, especially since futures were under pressure Friday in anticipation of a larger storage number, analysts said.
"Hog kills suffered because of storms in late January and slicers had to go to frozen (bellies) to fulfill their slicing needs," said Rich Tokheim at Investment Research Company.
USDA reported frozen belly stocks at 38.041 million lbs, below the low end of analysts' expectations of 39.7 to 43.2 million lbs.

Light hog kills resulted in late January when winter storms and bitter cold temperatures cut hog marketings, Tokheim noted. Some frozen pork bellies were sold as high as $71 per cwt to slicers who were hunting for product, he said.

Futures had shown weakness recently on concern that product had gone into storage despite a six percent reduction in the pace of hog slaughter. Much of this concern was based on reports coming from warehouses that report to the CME. But the report showed that non-reporting warehouses were moving product out as fast as reporting warehouses were putting it in.

"The report said even though we put 3.7 million lbs of bellies away in visible warehouses that report to the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, we were taking a duplicate amount, almost to the pound, out of warehouses that do not report to the exchange," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.

However, at least one analyst cited caution in view of the large rise in "other pork" on the report which could contain some pork bellies. The "other pork" total jumped 9.0 million lbs to 79.1 million.
"We could have some bellies in that unclassified (other pork) category," said Dale Benson, Vice President and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
Benson also noted the low trimmings figure of 32.5 million lbs versus 49.4 million last year which may account for the high price that packers are paying for slaughter sows.

Analysts agreed that the frozen beef number was bullish to cattle futures. Even though it was up from the previous month at 290.3 million lbs, it is down substantially from last year's 367.9 million lbs.
The large poultry number, over 1.0 billion lbs, will continue to offer competition to red meats.
